```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)


population_raw <- read.csv("/Users/ndtltd/Documents/Projects/Assigment K P/world_population.csv",
# population_raw <- read.csv("datasets/world_population.csv",
                           check.names = FALSE)

co2_raw <- read.csv("/Users/ndtltd/Documents/Projects/Assigment K P/CO2_emission.csv",
# co2_raw <- read.csv("datasets/CO2_emission.csv",
                    check.names = FALSE)

population <- population_raw |>
  rename(
    rank = Rank,
    code = CCA3,
    country_name = `Country/Territory`,
    continent = Continent,
    pop_2022 = `2022 Population`,
    pop_2020 = `2020 Population`,
    pop_2015 = `2015 Population`,
    pop_2010 = `2010 Population`,
    pop_2000 = `2000 Population`,
    pop_1990 = `1990 Population`,
    pop_1980 = `1980 Population`,
    pop_1970 = `1970 Population`,
    area_km2 = `Area (km²)`,
    density = `Density (per km²)`,
    growth_factor = `Growth Rate`,
    world_pct = `World Population Percentage`
  )

# The source repeats the 2019 column; retain its first copy.
co2_data <- co2_raw[, !duplicated(names(co2_raw)), drop = FALSE]
pop_names <- population |> select(code, country_name)
co2_data <- co2_data |>
  rename(country_source = `Country Name`, code = country_code) |>
  left_join(pop_names, by = "code", suffix = c("_source", "_population")) |>
  mutate(country_name = coalesce(country_name, country_source))

co2_years <- as.character(1990:2019)
co2_long <- co2_data |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(co2_years),
    names_to = "year",
    values_to = "co2_per_capita"
  ) |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(year))

merged <- population |>
  inner_join(co2_data, by = "country_name") |>
  mutate(co2_2019 = .data[["2019"]])

numeric_population <- names(population)[
  vapply(population, is.numeric, logical(1))
]
outlier_summary <- bind_rows(lapply(numeric_population, function(variable) {
  x <- population[[variable]]
  bounds <- quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE)
  spread <- bounds[2] - bounds[1]
  tibble(
    variable = variable,
    lower_bound = bounds[1] - 1.5 * spread,
    upper_bound = bounds[2] + 1.5 * spread,
    outlier_count = sum(x < bounds[1] - 1.5 * spread |
                          x > bounds[2] + 1.5 * spread, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}))

population <- population |>
  mutate(
    annual_growth_rate = growth_factor - 1,
    pop_2030 = pop_2022 * exp(annual_growth_rate * (2030 - 2022))
  )
top10 <- population |> arrange(desc(pop_2022)) |> slice_head(n = 10)
top10_trend <- top10 |>
  select(country_name, pop_1990, pop_2000, pop_2010, pop_2015,
         pop_2020, pop_2022) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("pop_"),
    names_to = "year",
    values_to = "population"
  ) |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(sub("pop_", "", year)))

top10_co2 <- co2_long |>
  filter(country_name %in% top10$country_name)

merged_complete <- merged |>
  filter(!is.na(co2_2019), !is.na(pop_2022))

correlation_data <- population |>
  select(area_km2, density, annual_growth_rate, world_pct)
correlation_matrix <- cor(correlation_data, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
correlation_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(correlation_matrix)) |>
  rename(variable_x = Var1, variable_y = Var2, correlation = Freq)

continent_totals <- merged |>
  filter(!is.na(co2_2019)) |>
  group_by(continent) |>
  summarise(sum_country_per_capita = sum(co2_2019), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(sum_country_per_capita))

population_co2_test <- cor.test(
  merged_complete$pop_2022, merged_complete$co2_2019,
  method = "pearson"
)
population_co2_model <- lm(
  co2_2019 ~ log10(pop_2022),
  data = merged_complete
)
```

# Introduction

This project explores how population size and growth relate to carbon dioxide
(CO2) emissions. It describes the supplied country-level population dataset,
projects 2030 population using the specified exponential formula, visualizes
population and emissions trends, and compares population with per-capita CO2
emissions.

# Data preparation and exploratory analysis

The population file contains `r nrow(population)` rows and
`r ncol(population_raw)` columns. The CO2 file contains
`r nrow(co2_raw)` rows and `r ncol(co2_raw)` columns before removing its
duplicate 2019 column. Population years are available at decadal or selected
intervals; CO2 emissions cover each year from 1990 through 2019. The CO2
measure is **metric tons per capita**, not total national emissions.

## Variable names and structure

```{r population-variables}
names(population_raw)
```

```{r population-structure}
str(population_raw)
```

```{r population-shape}
dim(population_raw)
```

## First five and last ten observations

```{r population-preview}
head(population_raw, 5)
tail(population_raw, 10)
```

## Duplicate rows and missing values

There are `r sum(duplicated(population_raw))` duplicate population rows.
No duplicate rows are removed unless present. Missing values by population
column are shown below.

```{r missing-population}
data.frame(
  variable = names(population_raw),
  missing_values = colSums(is.na(population_raw))
)
```

The population file has no missing observations, so no imputation or deletion
is needed. The CO2 file has `r sum(is.na(co2_data[["2019"]]))` missing 2019
emission values; missing CO2 observations are excluded from analyses requiring
that year rather than imputed.

## Outlier screening

The table uses the 1.5-IQR rule for selected quantitative variables. The
boxplots use a log scale for population, area, and density where that improves
readability. Countries with extreme but plausible population, area, or density
values are retained; they are not data errors and should not be deleted merely
because they are flagged by a boxplot.

```{r outlier-counts}
kable(outlier_summary, digits = 3,
      caption = "IQR-based outlier counts in selected population variables")
```

```{r outlier-boxplots, fig.height=9}
outlier_long <- population |>
  select(country_name, pop_2022, area_km2, density, growth_factor, world_pct) |>
  pivot_longer(-country_name, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value")
ggplot(outlier_long, aes(x = "", y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.45) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Value",
       title = "Distribution and IQR-flagged values") +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Population projection to 2030

The supplied `Growth Rate` is stored as a multiplicative annual factor (for
example, 1.01 represents approximately 1% growth). I therefore use
the annual decimal rate \(r = \text{Growth Rate} - 1\) and `t = 8` years in
`N[t] = P * exp(r * t)`, with 2022 population as `P`. This assumes a constant
rate through 2030 and is an illustrative projection, not an official forecast.

```{r projection-table}
top10 |>
  select(country_name, pop_2022, annual_growth_rate, pop_2030) |>
  mutate(across(c(pop_2022, pop_2030), round)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Country", "2022 population", "Annual rate", "Projected 2030"),
        caption = "Projection for the ten most populous countries")
```

# Population trends

## Ten most populous countries in 2022

```{r top10-population-2022}
ggplot(top10, aes(x = reorder(country_name, pop_2022), y = pop_2022)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2878B5") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Population",
       title = "Ten most populous countries, 2022") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Available population trend observations, 1990-2022

Population observations are available for 1990, 2000, 2010, 2015, 2020, and
2022; the lines connect these observed years and do not imply annual data.

```{r population-trends}
ggplot(top10_trend, aes(x = year, y = population,
                        color = country_name, group = country_name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1990, 2000, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2022)) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Population", color = "Country",
       title = "Population of the 2022 top ten, 1990-2022") +
  theme_minimal()
```

# CO2 emissions trend for the top ten

Country codes are used to harmonize country-name variants (for example,
different spellings or official names) before joining on canonical country
names. CO2 values are per capita. Missing country-year values remain missing
and are omitted from the corresponding line segments.

```{r co2-trends}
ggplot(top10_co2, aes(x = year, y = co2_per_capita,
                      color = country_name, group = country_name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "CO2 emissions (metric tons per capita)",
       color = "Country",
       title = "Per-capita CO2 emissions in the 2022 population top ten, 1990-2019") +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Correlation analysis

## Population characteristics

The correlations below describe linear association among area, density, annual
growth rate, and share of world population. Correlation does not establish
causation.

```{r population-correlations}
round(correlation_matrix, 3)
```

```{r population-correlation-heatmap}
ggplot(correlation_long, aes(variable_x, variable_y, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", correlation)), size = 4) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B",
    midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Correlation",
       title = "Population variable correlation heatmap") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1))
```

## 2022 population and 2019 CO2 emissions

The merged analysis includes `r nrow(merged_complete)` countries with both
2022 population and non-missing 2019 per-capita emissions. Pearson's
correlation is `r round(unname(population_co2_test$estimate), 3)`
(`r format.pval(population_co2_test$p.value, digits = 3)`). The regression
below uses log10 population because population is strongly right-skewed; it
describes association with per-capita emissions, not total emissions.

```{r population-co2-scatter}
ggplot(merged_complete,
       aes(x = pop_2022, y = co2_2019)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65, color = "#2878B5") +
  geom_smooth(aes(x = pop_2022), method = "lm", se = TRUE,
              formula = y ~ log10(x), color = "#B2182B") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "2022 population (log scale)",
       y = "2019 CO2 emissions (metric tons per capita)",
       title = "Population size and per-capita CO2 emissions") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r population-co2-model}
summary(population_co2_model)
```

# Comparison by continent

The requested continent comparison sums country-level 2019 per-capita values
within each continent. This is an unweighted sum of per-capita indicators; it
is **not** a continent's total CO2 emissions. A population-weighted estimate
or total-emissions dataset would be needed to compare total emissions properly.

```{r continent-table}
kable(continent_totals, digits = 2,
      col.names = c("Continent", "Sum of country per-capita values"),
      caption = "2019 CO2 metric tons per capita summed across available countries")
```

```{r continent-plot}
ggplot(continent_totals,
       aes(x = reorder(continent, sum_country_per_capita),
           y = sum_country_per_capita)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3A923A") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = "Sum of country per-capita values (metric tons per capita)",
       title = "2019 per-capita CO2 indicator sums by continent") +
  theme_minimal()
```

In the requested sum, the first continent is
**`r continent_totals$continent[1]`**
(`r round(continent_totals$sum_country_per_capita[1], 2)`).
The third is **`r continent_totals$continent[3]`**
(`r round(continent_totals$sum_country_per_capita[3], 2)`) and the last is
**`r continent_totals$continent[nrow(continent_totals)]`**
(`r round(continent_totals$sum_country_per_capita[nrow(continent_totals)], 2)`).
These values should be interpreted with the per-capita summation caveat above.

# Discussion, recommendations, and conclusion

Population grew substantially in several of the most populous countries, but
the exponential projection assumes each country's 2022 growth rate remains
constant. Population size alone is not a measure of per-capita emissions, and
the country-level association should not be interpreted as a causal effect.
The CO2 dataset also contains missing observations and reports emissions per
capita, limiting conclusions about total emissions. Future work should use
annual population data, document a forecast model and uncertainty, and obtain
total emissions or population-weighted per-capita emissions for fair
continent-level comparisons.

This analysis applies data inspection, cleaning, visualization, projection,
country matching, and correlation/regression methods. The main lesson is that
the meaning and units of a variable matter: summing per-capita values does not
produce total emissions.
